title: Liberation (1945)
hook: the camps are liberated, and survivors face a world that is gone

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah Senesh, and your line: the match that kindles. What did you light for someone else? Today, the gates open. Go gently with this one. Day one thousand nineteen.

Soldiers push open a gate. They came to fight a war, and nothing prepared them for what's inside: people too thin to stand, barracks full of the sick, a silence that doesn't sound like peace. On the other side of the gate, a prisoner hears that the guards are gone. Free. And almost at once, a second question arrives behind the first. Free to go where? To whom? Is anyone left? Today's word is the first half of that moment. We'll hold the second half too.
screen: `A GATE PUSHED OPEN.` → `FREE.` → `FREE TO GO WHERE?`

segments.voice: As the Allied armies crossed Europe, they reached the camps one after another. Soviet soldiers in the east, at places like Majdanek and Auschwitz. American and British soldiers in the west, at Buchenwald, Dachau, Bergen-Belsen. What they found, they photographed and filmed, and commanders ordered it recorded, so that no one could later say it hadn't happened. Liberation did not end the suffering at once. Soldiers handed out their own rations out of plain kindness: chocolate, tinned meat. But starving bodies could not take rich food, and some who had lived to see the gates open died in the days after. Doctors and nurses learned to feed people slowly. Then came the second question. Survivors went looking for family. They read lists, posted lists, wrote names on walls, asked every stranger from their town. Some walked back home to find no one waiting and strangers living in their houses. And yet, in the middle of all this, something else. At Bergen-Belsen, in the days after the British arrived, a Jewish army chaplain led a Sabbath service among the barracks. Survivors sang, and their voices were recorded. A psalm describes a return from exile in just this strange way: "When the LORD brought back those that returned to Zion, we were like unto them that dream." For those who lived it, liberation could feel like that. Real, and not yet believable. The word means being set free. It doesn't mean being made whole. Both are part of the story.
screen: `THE GATES OPEN.` · `FREED, BUT NOT YET SAFE.` · `NAMES ON LISTS, NAMES ON WALLS.` · `LIKE UNTO THEM THAT DREAM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of the survivors. Sit, and let your breath find its own pace. You don't need any picture of the camps. Instead, think of one survivor walking out through a gate, and the first ordinary things that came after. A bowl of soup. A clean shirt. A letter. A name found on a list. Hold that person gently, whoever they were. If you know a survivor's name, or a family story, bring it in. If you pray, you can pray for the survivors and for those who carry their memory. If you don't, simply keep them company in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Liberation. Being set free: the opening of the camps as the war in Europe ended, and the first slow steps of the people inside. Today's word.
Your line: set free, not yet whole. Today, notice one freedom you have that someone once had to fight for, and don't hurry past it. Day one thousand nineteen.

howItsDone: Jewish communities remember the liberation of the camps on Yom HaShoah and at memorial services, and some survivors and their families mark the day their own camp was liberated.

fork.setup: you're a soldier who has just opened a camp. starving prisoners reach toward you. you have your rations: chocolate, tinned meat. what do you do?
fork.reveal: soldiers did hand out their rations, out of kindness, and some starving people couldn't take the rich food. doctors and nurses learned to feed people slowly.

original.note: Hebrew: freedom. Passover is called the season of our freedom.

trapdoor: what you thought: the war ended and the prisoners went home.
what it means: set free, but sick, searching for family, and often with no home left to go to.
